title: Heirs in dhamma
hookLine: be my heirs in the teaching, not in material things (MN 3)

lines: THE CHINA, THE WATCH, THE RECIPE CARD.
cards: Families can fight over the strangest things after a funeral. Not only the house or the savings. The good china.
A watch. A recipe card in a grandmother's handwriting. What people inherit says something about who they were to the person who left.
The Buddha, very much alive, once told his monks exactly what he wanted them to inherit from him, and then gave an example to show he meant it.

teach.b: MN 3, the Dhammadayada, opens with one line: monks, be my heirs in the teaching, not my heirs in material things.

The word for material things is amisa: flesh, food, the things of the body, and sometimes bait. Then an example. Suppose, the Buddha says, I've finished my meal, and some food is left over, about to be thrown away.

Two monks arrive, hungry and weak. I tell them: eat it if you want; otherwise I'll throw it out. The first monk thinks: the Teacher said be heirs in the teaching, not in material things, and this food is a material thing.
So he goes without, and spends the night hungry and weak. The second eats, and spends the night comfortably.

And the Buddha says the first monk is more to be honored, because it will lead, for a long time, to fewness of wishes, contentment, effacement, ease in supporting oneself, and energy. It can be an uncomfortable example.
The point isn't that food is bad; it opens with the Buddha finishing his own meal. The point is what you reach for when something is offered, and what that habit hands down.
Then the Buddha goes into his dwelling, and Sariputta takes over, teaching how a teacher's disciples train in seclusion, or fail to.
The Dhammapada puts the value plainly, in Max Müller's translation: “The gift of the law exceeds all gifts.”

how: Buddhists often cite the Dhammapada line that the gift of the teaching exceeds all gifts, and in some communities giving or sponsoring copies of the teachings, or teaching others, is counted as a gift of dhamma.

o: an heir in the teaching, not in things
a gift of food offered to a teacher
a monk who gives away all his belongings

p: teaches after the Buddha goes in

s: MN 3 teaches that food is evil
the example opens with the Buddha's own meal; the point is what you reach for and hand down.
the Buddha calls the monk who went hungry more to be honored
for the sake of fewness of wishes and contentment.
flesh, food, worldly things, and the lure on a hook.

games.q: you're a hungry, weak monk. the Buddha offers you food he's about to throw away. what does the first monk in MN 3 do?
o: goes without, remembering 'heirs in the teaching'
games.why: he goes hungry that night, and the Buddha says he's the one more to be honored. the second monk, who ate, did nothing wrong; the story is about what each chose to carry forward.

practice: Think of one thing you hold onto that is only material, a purchase you keep circling, a comfort you reach for out of habit, and imagine setting it down.
Then pick up one teaching from these weeks to carry instead: the post holds, your own ground, seven ways, the useful question. Hold that one for the rest of the sit.

wordCard.voice: Dhamma-dayada, heir in the teaching. The Buddha's wish that his followers inherit his teaching, not his material things.

orig.note: Pali dhamma-dāyāda: heir in the dhamma, the teaching.

carryVoice: Your line: inherit the teaching. The best inheritance isn't a thing. Day four hundred five, done.

sources.q: The gift of the law exceeds all gifts

sources.ref: Anguttara Nikaya 2 (two kinds of gift, of things and of dhamma)
